Dinosaurs. Dinosaurs were a diverse group of reptiles that dominated terrestrial ecosystems for approximately one hundred sixty-five million years, from the Middle Triassic through the end of the Cretaceous Period about sixty-six million years ago. Ranging from pigeon-sized theropods to the largest land animals ever known, the sauropods, dinosaurs exhibited extraordinary morphological and behavioral variety and left a legacy as one of Earth's most successful vertebrate radiations.

Dinosaurs are divided into two major orders by hip structure. Saurischia, the lizard-hipped dinosaurs, includes theropods and sauropods. Ornithischia, the bird-hipped dinosaurs, were herbivorous and often ornate.

Theropods were bipedal carnivores. Tyrannosaurus rex is the archetypical apex predator, but small feathered theropods like Deinonychus and Velociraptor were sophisticated hunters.

Sauropods were the largest land animals. Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus, and Apatosaurus were herbivorous quadrupeds with long necks and tails, reaching lengths of over one hundred feet.

Ornithischians were exclusively herbivorous. Triceratops had a bony frill and horns for defense and display. Stegosaurus had dorsal plates and a spiked tail.

Dinosaurs were not ectothermic, or "cold-blooded," reptiles. Evidence from growth rates, bone structure, and ecological dominance suggests many were mesothermic or endothermic.

Modern birds are considered avian dinosaurs—the only dinosaur lineage to survive the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event sixty-six million years ago, which killed all non-avian dinosaurs.

Fossil trackways, nesting sites, and growth rings indicate complex social behavior, parental care, and possible gregariousness in many dinosaur groups.
